clinicalPearls: Caused by Oesophagostomum species, nodular worms of the large bowel, with human disease concentrated in parts of West Africa, notably northern Togo and Ghana
Acquired by ingesting infective larvae from soil or contaminated food and water, the larvae burrowing into the intestinal wall
The hallmark is formation of inflammatory nodules or abscesses in the colonic wall, which may coalesce into a palpable abdominal mass
The classic uninodular presentation, the Dapaong tumour, is a painful abdominal wall or intra-abdominal mass, while multinodular disease causes diffuse colitis-like symptoms
Presentations include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss and a palpable mass, often with marked eosinophilia
Diagnosis relies on imaging showing bowel wall nodules and on histology of excised or biopsied lesions; larvae may not appear in the stool
Treatment is with a benzimidazole anthelmintic such as albendazole, with surgical drainage or excision for large nodules or abscesses
reference.pathophysiology: Oesophagostomum species are nematodes related to hookworms whose natural hosts include primates, pigs and ruminants. Humans acquire infection by ingesting infective larvae from contaminated soil, food or water. In the intestine the larvae invade the wall of the colon and terminal ileum, where they encyst and provoke an intense inflammatory reaction. The host response forms characteristic granulomatous nodules and abscesses around the developing larvae, which may remain solitary as a large tumour-like mass or occur as multiple smaller nodules producing a colitis-like picture. Some larvae complete development, emerge into the lumen and mature into adult worms in the large bowel, while others remain trapped and die within the nodules. The inflammatory nodules account for the palpable masses, abdominal pain and, when they erupt or become secondarily infected, for abscess formation and local complications.
additionalDifferentials: Intestinal tuberculosis with an ileocaecal mass
Crohn's disease and other inflammatory bowel disease
Amoeboma or other infective mass lesion
Other tissue-invasive helminth infection with eosinophilia
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging or ultrasound demonstrating bowel wall nodules or an abdominal mass
Full blood count showing marked eosinophilia
Histopathology of excised or biopsied nodules identifying the larvae
Stool microscopy, recognising that eggs and larvae may be absent
Colonoscopy with biopsy when malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease is considered
Inflammatory markers and assessment for abscess formation
redFlags: A large or enlarging abdominal mass raising concern for malignancy or abscess
Signs of intestinal obstruction or perforation
Systemic sepsis from a secondarily infected nodule
Persistent symptoms after treatment prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good with anthelmintic treatment and, where needed, surgical management of nodules; complications such as large abscesses or obstruction increase morbidity but are usually treatable.
pitfalls: Mistaking a nodular mass for colonic carcinoma, tuberculosis or Crohn's disease
Relying on stool examination, which is frequently negative in tissue-dwelling disease
Overlooking the diagnosis in travellers or residents from endemic West African foci
Failing to drain or excise large abscesses in addition to giving anthelmintic therapy
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Anthelmintic therapy with a benzimidazole such as albendazole or mebendazole as the mainstay, with pyrantel pamoate as an alternative
Surgical excision or drainage of symptomatic nodules, abscesses (the Dapaong tumour) or an obstructing bowel mass
Supportive care for diarrhoea, abdominal pain and nutrition, with correction of associated losses
Confirm treatment response through resolution of eosinophilia and follow-up imaging of the bowel-wall nodules
Identify and treat complications such as large abscess formation or bowel obstruction
Public-health and preventive measures in endemic areas: safe food and water, sanitation and hand hygiene to prevent reinfection
